prompt: You've saved a broken version of a file over the working one with Ctrl+S. There's no version control set up. Is the working version recoverable?

options.text: No — Ctrl+S overwrote it, and nothing else was keeping a separate copy
Yes — undo history in your editor always keeps every save forever
Yes — the operating system automatically keeps every saved version of every file

hints: Ctrl+S doesn't create a new version — it replaces the old one on disk.
Editor undo history is usually cleared when you close the file or the editor, and isn't a permanent record.
explanation: Without a separate system deliberately keeping old versions, overwriting a file with Ctrl+S genuinely destroys the previous state — it isn't tucked away anywhere. Editor undo history feels like a safety net, but it's typically lost the moment you close the file, restart the editor, or sometimes just after enough new edits. Version control exists precisely because "the file is fine because I can undo" is not actually true once enough time or actions have passed.

prompt: True or false: once you've run git's one-time setup on a project, git automatically records a new version every time you save a file.

config.statement: Git automatically commits a new snapshot every time a tracked file is saved.
config.rubric: A full answer says false, and explains that git only records a snapshot when you explicitly stage and commit — saving alone never triggers it.

hints: Git can tell you a file changed since the last commit (git status) — that's different from recording a new commit.
Think about what two commands lesson 2 introduces for actually recording a snapshot.
explanation: False. Git never acts automatically — it will happily tell you a file has changed since the last commit (via `git status`), but recording an actual new snapshot always requires the deliberate two-step action of staging (`git add`) and committing (`git commit`). Nothing about saving a file in your editor talks to git at all.

prompt: Which commit message best follows the standard this lesson teaches — explaining why, not just restating what changed?

options.text: Fix: cart total showed $NaN when quantity field was left empty — added a default of 0
updated cart.js
more fixes
changed some numbers

hints: A good message names the actual bug or reason, specific enough to search for later.
"updated cart.js" is true but tells you nothing you couldn't already see from the file list itself.
explanation: The first message names the actual bug (NaN total), its trigger (empty quantity field), and the fix (a default of 0) — searchable and meaningful months later without opening the diff. The other three are all technically accurate but carry no real information: any of dozens of commits in a real project could honestly be described as "updated cart.js" or "more fixes."

prompt: Put these in the correct order to stage and commit only login.js, leaving an unfinished newFeature.js untouched:

items: git status
git add login.js
git status
git commit -m "Fix: login form accepted an empty password"

hints: Always check what's changed before staging anything.
Staging by filename lets you leave other changed files out entirely.
A second status check before committing confirms exactly what's about to be recorded.
explanation: Checking status first shows everything that's changed. Staging login.js specifically (not `git add .`) leaves newFeature.js completely out of the next snapshot. A second status check confirms exactly what's staged before committing — a real habit worth keeping, since committing is the point where the snapshot becomes permanent.

prompt: Match each situation to the command that actually fixes it:

pairs.left: Typo in the message of a commit you just made, not yet pushed
Ten minutes of uncommitted edits you want to throw away entirely
A bug from a commit three commits back that a teammate already pulled

hints: Amend only makes sense for your own most recent, still-private commit.
Restore only affects uncommitted changes — nothing already committed.
Revert adds new history rather than rewriting shared history.
explanation: Each situation has a different scope: amend rewrites your one most recent (private) commit; restore discards uncommitted edits that were never part of a commit at all; revert safely undoes an already-shared commit by adding a new corrective commit instead of rewriting the old one.

prompt: You run `git reset --hard HEAD~1` to undo your last commit. You also had an unrelated file open with fifteen minutes of uncommitted edits. What happens to those edits?

options.text: They're discarded too — --hard resets the whole working directory, not just the specific commit
They're untouched — --hard only affects the exact commit named
Git automatically saves them to a temporary backup file first

hints: "--hard" describes what happens to the working directory, not just the history.
Think about what "working directory" means versus "committed history."
explanation: --hard forces the entire working directory to match the target commit, discarding anything uncommitted along the way — whether or not it has anything to do with the commit you're undoing. This is exactly why it's the most dangerous common undo command: it does what it says, silently, with no automatic backup of what it throws away.

prompt: You create a branch with `git checkout -b experiment` and make five commits on it. Someone else, at the same time, is still working normally on main. What happens to main during this?

options.text: Nothing — main only changes from commits made while main is checked out; the experiment branch's commits don't touch it
Main gets all five commits automatically, since it's the default branch
Main is locked and can't be worked on until experiment is merged or deleted

hints: Branches are independent lines of commits from a shared starting point.
Nothing crosses between branches until a deliberate merge.
explanation: Commits only ever land on whichever branch is checked out at the time they're made. The experiment branch's five commits exist only on experiment — main is completely unaffected and can keep being worked on normally by anyone, the entire time. This independence is exactly what makes branches safe to abandon if an experiment doesn't work out.

prompt: Sort each line from a merge-conflict marker block by which branch's version it represents.

items.text: function saveData(entry) { localStorage.setItem('log', JSON.stringify(entry)); }
function saveData(entry) { return db.save('log', entry); }
>>>>>>> new-storage

hints: Everything between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= belongs to your current branch.
Everything between ======= and the >>>>>>> line belongs to the branch you're merging in.
explanation: <<<<<<< HEAD marks the start of your current branch's version, running down to the ======= divider. From ======= to >>>>>>> new-storage is the incoming branch's version. Resolving the conflict means choosing (or hand-combining) one final version and deleting all three marker lines before committing.

prompt: You've been committing carefully on your laptop for weeks with clean messages. What actually protects that work if the laptop is lost or destroyed tomorrow?

options.text: Nothing, unless it's also been pushed to a remote repository somewhere else
The commit history itself, since git keeps it permanently no matter what
Nothing needs to be done — GitHub automatically backs up any git repository that exists

hints: Ask where the .git folder holding that history physically lives.
"Permanent" history still only exists on whatever device is running it, unless copied elsewhere.
explanation: A perfect commit history is still just one copy in one place if it's never been pushed anywhere. Git doesn't automatically back anything up to the internet — that only happens when you deliberately connect a remote and push to it. Until then, the entire history is exactly as vulnerable as any other file on that one machine.

prompt: True or false: removing an API key from your current file and committing that removal fully protects the key going forward.

config.statement: Deleting a leaked secret from the current file and committing that change makes the secret safe.
config.rubric: A full answer says false and explains the key is still visible in the earlier commit that first added it, and needs to actually be rotated/invalidated.

hints: Git keeps every past commit as a permanent snapshot, not just the current state.
"Removed from the current file" and "removed from history" are two different things.
explanation: False. The commit that originally added the key is still sitting in the project's history, fully viewable — deleting it in a later commit doesn't erase that earlier snapshot. The only real fix is rotating the credential (making the leaked key invalid), not just editing it out of the current version.

prompt: You're about to make a risky, uncertain change to a project that currently works. What's the safest first move?

options.text: Create and switch to a new branch before making the change
Just start editing on main and commit as you go
Copy the whole project folder by hand into a `backup/` directory first

hints: A branch keeps main completely untouched while you experiment.
Editing straight on main means a bad experiment is now tangled into the branch you rely on.
explanation: Branching is exactly the tool for this: main stays untouched the entire time, so if the experiment fails, you switch back to main and lose nothing. Editing directly on main risks leaving it in a half-broken state; a manual backup folder is the pre-git habit this whole module exists to replace.

prompt: Put these in order to safely undo the most recent commit's message, which hasn't been pushed yet:

items: Run git commit --amend
Edit the commit message in the editor that opens
Save and close the editor

hints: --amend opens your default editor with the current message pre-filled.
Nothing changes until you save and close.
explanation: git commit --amend re-opens the most recent commit for editing — it opens your editor with the current message, you change it, save, and close, and the commit is updated in place. This only stays clean because the commit hasn't been shared with anyone yet.

prompt: True or false: git revert deletes the bad commit from the project's history.

config.statement: git revert deletes the original bad commit from history.
config.rubric: A full answer says false — revert adds a new commit that undoes the change, leaving the original commit still visible in history.

hints: Revert's whole point is not rewriting history.
Compare this to what reset does, which does rewrite history.
explanation: False. Revert adds a brand new commit that applies the opposite change — the original "bad" commit stays exactly where it is in the history, visible and unaltered. This is what makes revert safe to use on commits that have already been shared: nobody's copy of history gets rewritten.

prompt: Match each git term to what it actually does:

pairs.right: Stages a specific file to be included in the next commit
Permanently records everything currently staged, with a message
Sends local commits up to a connected remote repository
Brings commits from the remote down into your local copy

hints: Staging and committing are two separate steps, in that order.
Push sends your commits out; pull brings others' commits in — opposite directions.
explanation: These four cover the entire everyday git loop: stage what you want in the next snapshot, commit it with an explanation, then push it to a shared remote (or pull down what others pushed). Mixing up push and pull is the single most common beginner mistake — push goes out, pull comes in.

prompt: Sort each file by whether it belongs in .gitignore or should be committed normally.

items.text: .env holding a real API key
node_modules/ (thousands of regeneratable dependency files)
src/app.js — your actual application code
README.md explaining the project

hints: Secrets and huge regeneratable folders are the two classic .gitignore cases.
Your own actual source code and documentation are exactly what git exists to track.
explanation: node_modules and any file holding a real secret both belong in .gitignore — one because it's huge and regeneratable from a single command, the other because committing it means it's now permanently in history, recoverable forever even after "deleting" it. Your own source code and documentation are precisely what git is for tracking.

prompt: Two branches both changed the same line of the same file differently, and you run `git merge`. What does git do?

options.text: Stops and shows both versions marked with conflict markers, waiting for you to resolve it
Silently picks whichever branch has more total commits
Automatically combines both versions into one line of code

hints: Git only auto-merges when changes don't overlap — this is the case where they do.
Think about what you actually saw in the spot-flaw exercise in lesson 4.
explanation: When two branches genuinely disagree about the same lines, git can't safely guess which is correct — it stops, inserts both versions clearly marked with <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>>, and waits for a human to resolve it. It never silently picks a winner or blends code automatically; that would risk producing something neither branch actually intended.

prompt: You committed a bug fix and a half-finished experiment together in one commit, `git add .` used by habit. Explain, in your own words, how you'd split this into two clean commits using what this module taught — you can't undo the commit yet, assume you're about to make the next one correctly instead.
hints: Think about what staging lets you choose, going forward.
The goal here isn't undoing the past commit — it's not repeating the mistake on the next one.
explanation: A strong answer describes staging deliberately by filename (or by hunk) instead of using `git add .` out of habit — checking `git status` first, staging only the files (or specific changes) that belong to one logical change, committing that with a specific message, then staging and committing the rest separately. The core idea: staging is the tool that lets unrelated changes become separate, honest commits instead of one tangled one.

prompt: Your laptop's hard drive fails completely, with no other copy of your project anywhere. What's the actual state of your work?

options.text: Entirely lost, if the project was never pushed to a remote repository
Recoverable from git's history, since git never really deletes anything
Recoverable, since GitHub automatically syncs any local git repository

hints: Git's history lives on the device running it, unless deliberately copied elsewhere.
"git never deletes history" is true only within that one local .git folder.
explanation: Git's promise to keep every commit is a promise about that one repository's history, wherever it physically lives — it says nothing about surviving the device itself failing. Without a remote (a genuinely separate copy, pushed there on purpose), a destroyed laptop takes the entire history with it. This is the exact scenario lesson 5 exists to prevent.

prompt: A project has four hand-tested features. Three weeks later, one change to shared code silently breaks a feature nobody re-checked. What's the actual gap manual testing left here?

options.text: It only verifies what you deliberately re-check at the moment you check it — it can't protect features you're not currently looking at
Manual testing is fundamentally less accurate than automated testing, even at the exact moment it's performed
The developer simply wasn't careful enough this time

hints: Think about what manual testing actually covers, versus what it would need to cover to catch this.
The gap is structural, not about carefulness.
explanation: Manual testing is perfectly accurate for the thing you're actively checking right now — the gap is that it has no memory and doesn't re-run itself. A change to shared code can silently affect a feature built weeks ago that nobody thinks to re-click through, because nothing is prompting anyone to. That's a structural limit of manual checking, not a carelessness problem.

prompt: True or false: an automated test written today will still catch a regression caused by a completely unrelated change made weeks from now.

config.statement: A test written today still catches a regression from an unrelated change made weeks later.
config.rubric: A full answer says true, and explains that the test re-runs the exact same check every time regardless of what else changed.

hints: A test doesn't know or care what else was edited — it just re-checks its one specific thing.
This is the actual advantage over manual testing described in this lesson.
explanation: True. The test doesn't need to know anything changed elsewhere — it just re-runs the exact same check, every time you run the suite, regardless of what else was edited. That's precisely what makes it catch regressions manual testing misses: it doesn't depend on anyone remembering to re-check that specific feature.

prompt: Which of these is a complete, meaningful automated test for a function celsiusToFahrenheit that should return 32 for input 0?

options.text: test('converts 0 celsius correctly', () => { expect(celsiusToFahrenheit(0)).toBe(32); });
test('converts celsius', () => { celsiusToFahrenheit(0); });
test('converts celsius', () => { expect(true).toBe(true); });

hints: A real test needs all three parts: input, the actual call, and an assertion about the real expected result.
Calling a function without asserting anything about its return value doesn't check whether it's correct.
explanation: The first option has all three required parts: a known input (0), a real call to the function, and a specific assertion (toBe(32)) about the expected result. The second calls the function but never checks its output — it would pass no matter what celsiusToFahrenheit returns. The third doesn't even call the real function; it just asserts something trivially true.

prompt: Put these in order for writing and running a first test for applyDiscount(100, 10):

items: Import test and expect from the testing library
Call applyDiscount(100, 10) and store the result
Assert the result with expect(result).toBe(90)
Run the test command and read the pass/fail output

hints: You need the tools imported before you can use them.
The call happens before you can assert anything about its result.
Nothing is verified until you actually run the test.
explanation: The standard order: import the testing tools, call the real function with a known input, assert what the result should be, then run the suite and read what it actually reports. Skipping the last step means the test exists but has never actually verified anything.

prompt: Sort each test case for applyDiscount(price, percent) by whether it's the happy path or a genuine edge case.

items.text: applyDiscount(100, 10) — a normal price, normal discount
applyDiscount(100, 100) — a full 100% discount
applyDiscount(100, -10) — a negative discount
applyDiscount(0, 10) — a price of zero

hints: The happy path is the one case every naive implementation is already built to handle.
Zero, negative, and maximum values are the classic edge cases.
explanation: applyDiscount(100, 10) is the ordinary, expected case — worth having, least likely to reveal a bug. The other three are edges: a 100% discount tests whether the result correctly lands at exactly 0, a negative percent tests whether invalid input is rejected instead of raising the price, and a zero price tests a boundary an implementation might not have considered at all.

prompt: A function meant to apply free shipping for orders of $50 or more is written as `if (total > 50) return true;`. What does this return for a total of exactly 50, and is that correct?

options.text: false — which is wrong, since "50 or more" should include exactly 50
true — and that's correct
It throws an error, since 50 is an edge case

hints: `>` is strictly greater than — check what happens at the exact boundary value.
"50 or more" needs >=, not >.
explanation: `total > 50` excludes 50 itself, since > means strictly greater than. For a total of exactly 50, this returns false — incorrect, since the rule was "$50 or more," which should include 50 exactly. This is the same > vs >= boundary bug from the lesson, just with a different threshold and function.

prompt: Which assertion would still pass even if isPalindrome('racecar') were broken and always returned false?

options.text: expect(isPalindrome('racecar')).toBeDefined();
expect(isPalindrome('racecar')).toBe(true);
expect(isPalindrome('racecar')).toEqual(true);

hints: toBeDefined() only checks that something came back — false is still "defined."
toBe(true) and toEqual(true) both require the exact value true, which a broken function returning false would fail.
explanation: toBeDefined() only checks the result isn't undefined — false is a perfectly defined value, so this assertion passes regardless of whether the function is actually correct. toBe(true) and toEqual(true) both require the specific value true, so either genuinely fails if the function is broken and returns false instead — which is exactly what makes them meaningful.

prompt: You wrote a test: expect(applyDiscount(100, 10)).toBe(90), and it passes. Describe, step by step, exactly how you'd prove this test is genuinely meaningful rather than just accidentally green.
hints: The proof isn't in reading the code — it's in watching the test's behavior change.
Think about what has to happen to the real implementation, temporarily, and what you'd expect to see.
explanation: A strong answer: temporarily edit the real applyDiscount function so it's clearly wrong (for example, make it always return the original price unchanged, or subtract the wrong percentage), re-run the test, and confirm it now fails — specifically showing 'expected 90, received' something else. Then revert the deliberate change and re-run to confirm it passes again on the real, correct code. Watching it go red on broken code and green again on correct code is the actual proof; never having seen it fail is not.

prompt: A project has twelve tests across four files. What's the main advantage of a single command that runs all of them, over running each file separately?

options.text: It removes any judgment call about which tests "probably matter" for a given change — you just run everything, every time
It's the only way to see whether any test failed
It runs the tests faster than running them individually would

hints: The value isn't really about speed — it's about not having to decide anything.
Running files individually gives the same information, just with more friction and more chances to skip something.
explanation: The real value of one command for the whole suite is removing the judgment call — "I'll just run the tests I think are relevant" is exactly the reasoning that lets regressions slip through in unrelated files. A single command with zero decisions to make is what actually gets run consistently, every time.

prompt: A test fails with 'expected 90, received 100'. Put these steps in the sensible order for responding to it:

items: Read the expected vs. received values in the failure message
Form a hypothesis about what the gap (100 instead of 90) suggests is happening
Check the relevant part of the code against that hypothesis
Make a fix and re-run the test to confirm it now passes

hints: Reading the message comes before guessing at a fix.
The gap itself (unchanged value) is a real clue worth reasoning about before opening any code.
A fix isn't confirmed until the test is re-run and actually passes.
explanation: Reading the specific expected-vs-received gap first (100, the unchanged original price, instead of 90) points toward a specific hypothesis — the discount math likely isn't running at all — before you've opened a single file. Checking code against a hypothesis is faster than scanning randomly, and re-running the test is what actually confirms the fix, rather than assuming it worked.

prompt: A function `isEven(n)` should return true for even numbers. Which test is meaningful, not decorative?

options.text: expect(isEven(4)).toBe(true);
expect(isEven(4)).toBeDefined();
expect(typeof isEven(4)).toBe(typeof isEven(4));

hints: A meaningful assertion checks a specific, correct value.
toBeDefined() and comparing a value to itself both pass regardless of correctness.
explanation: expect(isEven(4)).toBe(true) is the only one that would actually fail if isEven were broken — it checks the specific correct value. toBeDefined() only checks something came back, and comparing a value's type to its own type is trivially always true, checking nothing about correctness.

prompt: Put these in order to write a first test for a function square(n) that should return 9 for input 3:

items: import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
const result = square(3);
expect(result).toBe(9);

hints: Import before use.
Call before asserting on the result.
explanation: Standard shape: import the tools, call the real function with the known input, then assert the specific expected result. Skipping or reordering any step either breaks the test or leaves it not actually checking anything.

prompt: True or false: a function that has one passing happy-path test has been adequately tested.

config.statement: One passing happy-path test is enough to call a function adequately tested.
config.rubric: A full answer says false, and names at least one kind of edge case (zero, negative, empty, boundary) still worth testing.

hints: The happy path is the least likely case to reveal a bug.
Think about what kinds of input the function might mishandle that a normal case wouldn't reveal.
explanation: False. The happy path confirms the function works under ordinary conditions, but says nothing about zero, negative numbers, empty input, or exact boundary values — the cases most likely to reveal a real bug, since they're the ones an implementation is least likely to have been naturally built to handle correctly.

prompt: Match each test-quality problem to what's actually wrong with it:

pairs.right: Passes for almost any output — doesn't check correctness, just existence
Misses edge cases most likely to reveal a real bug

pairs.left: Never watching the test fail on broken code
pairs.right: No proof the test would actually catch a real bug

pairs.left: Testing age > 65 instead of age >= 65's boundary
pairs.right: Boundary bug invisible to tests on either side of the line

hints: Each problem here maps to a specific gap covered in this module's lessons.
Think about what each weak test would still let slip through unnoticed.
explanation: Each of these is a distinct way a test suite can look fine while actually protecting very little: a weak assertion that passes regardless of output, coverage that only checks the easy case, a test never proven capable of failing, and a boundary condition nobody actually tested at the exact threshold value.

prompt: Sort each proposed test case for a shipping-cost function by whether it's happy path or a genuine edge case.

items.text: A normal 2kg package to a standard address
A 0kg package (empty order)
A package weighing exactly the maximum allowed
A negative weight (a data-entry error)

hints: The happy path is the case every implementation naturally gets right first.
Zero, the exact maximum, and invalid negative values are the classic edges.
explanation: Only the normal 2kg package is the happy path — comfortable, expected, least likely to reveal a bug. Zero weight, the exact maximum boundary, and a negative (invalid) weight are all genuine edges a real implementation might mishandle, each for a different reason.

prompt: You break a function on purpose to test your test, and the test still passes on the broken code. What does this tell you?

options.text: The test isn't actually checking the thing you think it's checking, and needs fixing before you can trust it
The function must not really be broken, despite your edit
This is expected — most tests are supposed to pass regardless of the implementation

hints: The whole point of the deliberate-break check is to see whether the test can fail at all.
A test that stays green on code you know is broken has a real problem.
explanation: If you've deliberately broken the code and the test still passes, the test isn't actually verifying what you think — it's either asserting something too weak (like toBeDefined()) or not really exercising the changed code path at all. This is exactly the signal to fix the test, not evidence the code is secretly fine.

prompt: A teammate says: 'We have 40 tests and they're all green, so we're covered.' Using this module's ideas, explain what's still missing from that statement, and how you'd actually check.
hints: Green tests alone don't tell you what they're actually asserting.
Think about the two separate checks this module teaches: are the right cases covered, and would each test actually fail on broken code?
explanation: A strong answer notes that 'all green' says nothing about whether the assertions are meaningful (not toBeDefined()-style checks), whether edge cases are covered alongside the happy path, or whether each test has actually been proven capable of failing by breaking the code on purpose. The number of passing tests is not itself evidence of coverage or correctness — what matters is what each test actually checks and whether it's been verified to catch a real break.

prompt: A test fails: 'expected true, received false' for isPalindrome('racecar'). What's the most useful next step?

options.text: Read the failure as a real clue — a true palindrome returning false suggests the comparison logic itself is wrong, and check that specifically
Immediately delete the test since it's clearly the test that's wrong
Add a second, identical test and see if that one passes instead

hints: Expected vs. received tells you the direction of the problem, not just that something's wrong.
'racecar' being a genuine palindrome that returned false points at the actual comparison logic.
explanation: The failure message is specific: a genuine palindrome ('racecar') came back false, which points directly at the comparison logic itself rather than, say, an input-handling issue. Deleting the test removes the information instead of using it; adding a duplicate test doesn't investigate anything — reading the actual gap and following it into the code is the fastest path to the real bug.

prompt: A 900-line app.js mixes login, discount, and API code together, and finding any one feature means scrolling past the other two. A brand-new 40-line single-feature script does not have this problem. Which one has a real, concrete reason to be split?

options.text: The 900-line app.js — there's a pointable cost (scrolling past unrelated code) that splitting directly removes
Both equally — any project benefits from being split into multiple files
Neither — splitting files is mostly a matter of personal taste

hints: Look for a concrete, describable cost, not just a feeling that "bigger should be split."
The 40-line script doesn't have the scrolling-past-unrelated-code problem at all yet.
explanation: The 900-line file has an actual, nameable cost: finding one feature requires wading through code for two others that have nothing to do with it. The 40-line script has no such cost yet — splitting it would add files to track without removing any real friction. The reason to split is always a concrete problem you can point to, not a size threshold or a general rule.

prompt: True or false: creating a full folder structure (utils/, components/, services/, helpers/) before a project has more than a couple of real files makes it easier to work in.

config.statement: Creating a full folder structure before a project has enough code to fill it makes the project easier to work in.
config.rubric: A full answer says false, and explains that spreading a small amount of code across many folders adds navigation overhead without removing any real problem yet.

hints: With very little real code, ask what problem the folders are actually solving.
Premature structure trades a problem you don't have for one you do — remembering where things are.
explanation: False. With only a handful of real pieces of code, spreading them across many mostly-empty folders means remembering which folder holds which small thing, which is often harder than just scrolling a short single file. The structure isn't wrong forever — it earns its keep once there's enough real code that grouping it saves more than it costs.

prompt: You move a function out of app.js into discount.js. What's the one line in discount.js that makes the function usable from app.js at all?

options.text: export function applyDiscount(...) { ... }
function applyDiscount(...) { ... }
import { applyDiscount } from './app.js';

hints: Without export, a function is trapped inside the file it's defined in.
import is what app.js needs to use it — but discount.js needs export first.
explanation: export is what marks a function as usable from other files — without it, applyDiscount would be defined in discount.js but completely inaccessible anywhere else, even with a correct import elsewhere. The plain function declaration alone (no export) keeps it private to that file; the import line belongs in app.js, not discount.js.

prompt: Sort each way of splitting a 900-line file by whether it's a genuine split (by responsibility) or an arbitrary one (by line count).

items.text: login.js, discount.js, api.js — each holds everything related to one responsibility
part1.js (lines 1-300), part2.js (lines 301-600), part3.js (lines 601-900)
validateForm.js, containing only form-validation logic
earlyStuff.js and laterStuff.js, split at whatever point felt convenient

hints: A genuine split means a file's name tells you what's inside it.
An arbitrary split can still scatter related code across every resulting file.
explanation: login.js/discount.js/api.js and validateForm.js are genuine splits — each groups code by what it's actually responsible for, so a bug in one area has exactly one place to look. part1/part2/part3 and earlyStuff/laterStuff are arbitrary — they're technically multiple files, but related code can still be scattered across all of them, so the real confusion doesn't actually go away.

prompt: A file holding signup-form validation logic is named utils.js. Four months later, what's the actual cost of this name?

options.text: Finding the validation logic means opening files and guessing, since "utils" gives no clue what's inside
There's no real cost — utils.js is a standard, expected name in any project
The cost is only that the file looks unprofessional, nothing practical

hints: A file name is a promise about contents, read before opening it.
"Utils" is vague enough to plausibly hold almost anything.
explanation: "utils.js" could plausibly contain almost any small helper function, which means it gives zero information about what's actually inside — finding the signup validation logic later means opening files and checking, one by one, instead of guessing correctly from the name. This is a real, practical cost (time spent searching), not just an aesthetic one.

prompt: A project has userProfile.js, UserSettings.js, and user-preferences.js — three different casing styles for files about the same general subject. What's the actual problem this creates?

options.text: You can't predict a file's exact name from memory, because the casing style varies with no pattern
JavaScript will fail to run with mixed casing styles in file names
There's no real problem — as long as each individual name is descriptive, the casing doesn't matter

hints: Consistency is what makes a name predictable, not just descriptiveness alone.
Think about what happens when you try to type a filename from memory.
explanation: Each of these names is individually descriptive — the problem is that the casing style varies with no pattern, so you can't reliably guess or type the exact filename from memory; you have to check every time. JavaScript itself doesn't care about casing consistency, but the person searching the project does.

prompt: A fetch call is hardcoded as fetch('http://localhost:3000/api/users'). It works locally and fails once deployed. What's the actual issue?

options.text: localhost:3000 means "this specific machine" — correct during local development, meaningless once the code runs somewhere else
The URL contains a spelling mistake
fetch() is not supported on deployed servers

hints: localhost isn't a typo — it's a value that's genuinely correct in exactly one environment.
Ask what the correct value should be on a live server, versus your laptop.
explanation: "localhost" correctly refers to whichever machine is currently running the code — true and useful during local development, and meaningless (or pointing at the wrong machine entirely) once deployed elsewhere. This is exactly why environment-specific values belong in configuration, read at runtime, rather than hardcoded directly into the code.

prompt: A teammate hardcodes a real, working API key directly into a JavaScript file so the app 'just works' without extra setup. Explain, using this module's ideas, what's actually risky about this beyond it being inconvenient to change later.
hints: Think about who can read a file directly, and what happens if it's ever committed to git.
This connects back to what the version-control module taught about secrets in commit history.
explanation: A strong answer explains that a hardcoded key is exposed to anyone who can read the code — a teammate, anyone who clones the repository, and permanently in git history the moment it's committed, even if later deleted. The fix is reading it from an environment variable at runtime, with the real value kept in a .env file that's excluded from version control via .gitignore — so the actual secret never appears in the code or the repository at all.

prompt: A README says: 'A tool for tracking daily symptoms and viewing trends. Built with JavaScript.' A stranger clones the repo. What's missing for them to actually run it?

options.text: Specific setup steps — what to install, what environment variables are needed, and the exact command to start it
Nothing — a clear description is sufficient for anyone who knows JavaScript
A longer, more detailed description of the app's features

hints: Knowing what a project does isn't the same as knowing how to run this specific one.
Install steps, required config, and the run command are specific to this project and can't be guessed.
explanation: The description explains what the project is, but says nothing about which command installs its dependencies, which environment variables it needs (and where to get real values), or which command actually starts it — all specific to this project and unguessable from a general description alone, regardless of how familiar the reader is with JavaScript in general.

prompt: Put these in the sensible order for verifying a README actually works, once written:

items: Write the setup steps as a numbered list
Attempt to follow the steps yourself as if you'd never seen the project
Note every point where you had to fill in a step from memory that wasn't written down
Add the missing steps to the README and re-test

hints: Writing the steps comes first, but writing them isn't the same as verifying they work.
The gaps only show up when you try to actually follow your own instructions, not when you re-read them.
explanation: Writing steps down is necessary but not sufficient — the real test is attempting to follow them as a stranger would, noticing every place you silently relied on knowledge that isn't actually written in the README, then closing those gaps and re-testing. Skipping the follow-along step is exactly how READMEs end up complete-looking but not actually usable.

prompt: A project has one file, calculator.js, 60 lines, doing one job well. Should it be split into multiple files right now?

options.text: No — there's no concrete cost yet (no scrolling past unrelated code, nothing tangled) that splitting would remove
Yes — any file over 50 lines should be split for good practice
Yes — professional projects always use multiple files

hints: Look for an actual, nameable cost the split would remove.
A single well-organized 60-line file doing one job has no scrolling-past-unrelated-code problem.
explanation: There's no concrete problem here to fix — one file, one clear job, nothing tangled or hard to find. Splitting now would add files to track without removing any real friction, which is exactly the premature-structure cost from lesson 1.

prompt: Sort each of these by whether it's a genuine reason to split code into a new file, or not yet a real reason.

items.text: A function is used identically in three different places, and you keep scrolling to find its one definition
The file has reached exactly 100 lines
Two clearly unrelated features are tangled together in one file, making each hard to find
You want the project to look more organized to whoever sees it

hints: A genuine reason is a concrete cost you can point to.
Line count alone and appearances aren't concrete costs.
explanation: Repeated, hard-to-find code and genuinely tangled unrelated features are real, pointable costs splitting removes. An arbitrary line-count threshold and wanting to look organized aren't concrete problems — they're the premature-structure trap from lesson 1, trading a problem you don't have for navigation overhead you don't need yet.

prompt: Put these in order to move a formatDate function out of app.js into its own module, dateUtils.js:

items: Move the function definition into dateUtils.js
Add export in front of the function in dateUtils.js
Add an import for formatDate at the top of app.js
Call formatDate(...) exactly as before

hints: The function has to physically move before it can be exported from its new location.
export happens where the function is defined; import happens where it's used.
explanation: The function moves first, then gets exported from its new home, then gets imported wherever it's used — after which the call site itself doesn't change at all. This mirrors the worked example exactly, just with a different function.

prompt: A folder is named misc/ and contains a date formatter, a login helper, and a discount calculator — three unrelated things. What does this name actually communicate?

options.text: Nothing useful — "misc" signals these are things nobody decided where to properly put, not a real category
That everything inside is optional and safe to delete
That everything inside is related by being small utility functions

hints: "misc" (and similar catch-alls) is the folder-naming equivalent of "utils.js" — vague by definition.
The three items listed aren't actually related to each other in any real way.
explanation: "misc" doesn't describe a real shared responsibility — it's where things go when nobody wanted to decide where they actually belonged. A date formatter, a login helper, and a discount calculator have nothing meaningfully in common; grouping them under a name that says "miscellaneous" gives a future reader zero information about what any specific one of them does.

prompt: True or false: an API key that's read from an environment variable, with the real value stored only in a .env file listed in .gitignore, is safe even if the project's repository is later made public.

config.statement: An API key handled this way stays safe even if the repository later becomes public.
config.rubric: A full answer says true, and explains that the real key value was never committed — only code that reads an environment variable was, so nothing secret is exposed by making the repo public.

hints: The question is whether the actual secret value ever entered git history at all.
.gitignore prevents .env from being committed in the first place — not just hidden after the fact.
explanation: True, assuming the setup was done correctly from the start: the code itself only ever references process.env.API_KEY (or similar) — a variable name, not a secret value — and the actual key lives solely in a local .env file that .gitignore has kept out of every commit. Making the repository public exposes the code, but the code never contained the real secret to begin with.

prompt: Match each project value to where it belongs:

pairs.left: A function that calculates shipping cost

pairs.right: Configuration (environment variable, kept out of git)

pairs.left: The logic that renders a page's layout

hints: Configuration values change depending on where the code runs.
Code is the same everywhere it runs — only the values it depends on change.
explanation: Connection URLs and API keys are environment-specific — different (and in the key's case, secret) depending on where the code is running, so they belong in configuration. The shipping calculation and layout logic behave identically no matter what environment runs them, which is exactly what makes them code rather than configuration.

prompt: You're handed a project with one README line: 'A budget tracker app.' Using this module's standard, write the setup section it's missing — describe, in your own words, the categories of information a real setup section needs, even without knowing this specific project's exact tech stack.
hints: Think about the actual gaps a stranger would hit, in order, trying to run an unfamiliar project.
Installation, configuration, and the run command are the three recurring categories from this lesson.
explanation: A strong answer names the missing categories: what to install and how (a package manager command), what configuration or environment variables are required and where real values come from (or a .env.example reference), the exact command that starts the project, and what a successful result looks like once it's running. The specific commands would depend on the real tech stack, but the categories — install, configure, run, confirm — are what any real setup section needs regardless of stack.

prompt: You open a 40-file unfamiliar project to fix one bug. Which is the more efficient first move?

options.text: Find the entry point and skim what it calls, to see the overall shape
Start reading every file in file-explorer order from the top
Open files at random until something looks related to the bug

hints: The entry point is the one file guaranteed to matter, since everything starts from there.
File-explorer order and random exploration have no relationship to how the code actually runs.
explanation: The entry point is guaranteed to be relevant, since every run of the program starts there — following what it calls builds a real map in the order things actually execute. File-explorer order and random browsing both have no relationship to how the code runs, so neither reliably leads anywhere useful.

prompt: True or false: to safely fix one specific bug in an unfamiliar project, you need to first fully understand every file in it.

config.statement: Fixing one specific bug safely requires first fully understanding every file in the project.
config.rubric: A full answer says false, and explains that following the one specific thread the bug touches is the real, bounded skill — not full comprehension of the whole project.

hints: Most real bugs touch a small fraction of a real project.
"Understand everything first" is a standard nobody, including experienced developers, actually meets before making changes.
explanation: False. Most bugs and small changes touch a specific, traceable thread through a small part of the project — the actual skill is following that thread to its source, not comprehending the entire codebase first. Requiring full understanding before any change would mean never actually starting.

prompt: A "Sale ends today!" banner shows even though the sale ended last week. Put these tracing steps in order:

items: Search the project for the exact text "Sale ends today"
Find the condition or variable that controls whether it renders
Trace where that condition's value actually comes from
Identify the specific line where the date comparison is wrong

hints: Start from something concrete and searchable — the exact visible text.
The message itself isn't the bug; whatever decides whether it shows is the next thread to pull.
explanation: Starting from the literal, searchable text narrows the search immediately. From there, finding what controls whether it renders, then tracing that control's actual source, is what leads to the real bug — usually a date comparison, similar to the free-shipping threshold example in the lesson.

prompt: A cart total displays as $NaN. Which starting point for tracing the bug is most likely to actually work?

options.text: Find where the total is calculated, then check each value that calculation depends on
Assume the math operator (+ or *) is wrong and start rewriting the calculation from scratch
Search the codebase for the literal text "NaN"

hints: $NaN is a computed result, not text that exists anywhere in the source code.
Tracing backward from the calculation to its inputs is what actually finds the non-numeric value.
explanation: NaN is a runtime result, not source text — searching for it directly is a dead end. Tracing backward from the calculation to each value it depends on is what actually finds the culprit, which (as covered in the storing-data and JavaScript modules) is very often an unconverted string input rather than a broken operator.

prompt: Searching an unfamiliar project for "discount" returns 140 results across 30 files. What's the better next search term, if the actual function name applyDiscount is visible in an error message?

options.text: applyDiscount — a specific identifier likely to return a small, relevant set of results
A wider search like "discount code" to be extra thorough
The literal wrong output value you're seeing on screen

hints: A specific function name is far more precise than a generic word.
Wider searches return more noise, not more clarity.
explanation: applyDiscount, an actual specific identifier, is likely to appear in only a few, directly relevant places — its definition and its call sites — unlike the generic word "discount," which matches comments, unrelated variables, and unrelated features. A wider search would return even more noise, and a literal output value almost never appears in source code at all.

prompt: You see a call to formatUserName(user) and, based on the name, assume it just returns a formatted string with no other effects. What's the risk of proceeding without checking its actual definition?

options.text: The function's real behavior might include something the name doesn't mention, like a side effect — only the actual code is a reliable source of truth
There's no risk — function names always exactly describe everything a function does
The only risk is a minor performance cost, not a correctness one

hints: Names are written by people and can drift from what the code actually does.
Jump-to-definition exists precisely because guessing from a name is a real, common way to miss something.
explanation: A function's actual behavior is defined by its code, not by its name — in an unfamiliar project you didn't write, there's a real chance the name doesn't capture everything it does, including side effects. Jumping to the actual definition is the only reliable way to know what will really happen when it's called.

prompt: While fixing one specific bug in unfamiliar code, you also notice an outdated comment and an inconsistent variable name nearby. What's the safer move?

options.text: Fix only the one bug you were asked about; note the other issues separately without changing them in the same edit
Fix everything you noticed in one combined change, since you're already in the file
Skip the bug fix too, since the file clearly needs a larger cleanup first

hints: Each additional unrelated change is its own chance to break something you don't fully understand yet.
A scoped change is also easier to debug if something does go wrong.
explanation: In code you don't yet deeply understand, each unrelated change bundled in is an additional risk and makes any resulting bug harder to isolate. The safer move is fixing exactly the one thing you were asked about, and separately noting other issues you noticed — not ignoring them forever, just not touching them in the same change.

prompt: Sort each verification step by whether it gives real evidence a fix is correct, or just a false sense of confidence.

items.text: Running the specific case you fixed and confirming correct behavior
Reading the changed line and confirming it looks right, without running anything
Running a case that should NOT trigger the fix, confirming it still doesn't
Assuming it's fine since the change was small

hints: Actually running behavior, not just reading it, is what produces real evidence.
Change size alone says nothing about whether the change is correct.
explanation: Actually running the fixed case and a non-triggering case gives real, observed evidence the change behaves correctly in both directions. Reading a line and feeling confident, or assuming a small change must be safe, are both the same kind of false confidence a weak test like toBeDefined() gives — they feel like checking without actually confirming anything.

prompt: You read a function using .filter() and .map(), both familiar syntax. What does recognizing this syntax actually tell you about whether it's safe to change?

options.text: Very little on its own — you'd still need to predict its actual output for a real input to know you understand it
It confirms full understanding, since the syntax itself is the hard part
Nothing — familiar syntax is actually a red flag for hidden bugs

hints: Recognizing syntax and predicting behavior for specific data are two different tests.
This function's specific logic and data could still behave unexpectedly even with fully familiar syntax.
explanation: Recognizing .filter() and .map() as familiar syntax says nothing about what this specific function does with this specific data — the real test is being able to predict its output for a real input, ideally an edge case, without running it. Familiar syntax isn't a red flag either; it's simply not the same thing as understanding the logic built from it.

prompt: You're reading an unfamiliar function and realize you can't confidently predict what it returns for an empty input. Describe, using this module's ideas, what you'd actually do next — not give up, not guess and change the code anyway.
hints: The rest of this module gave you real tools for exactly this situation.
Think about tracing, jump-to-definition, and testing a prediction deliberately.
explanation: A strong answer describes using this module's actual tools: tracing the specific unclear part of the logic (lesson 2), jumping to the real definition of anything being guessed at rather than assumed (lesson 3), and — importantly — running the function with the empty input as a deliberate, isolated experiment to see the real result, rather than guessing blindly inside a change to production code. Not understanding something yet is a normal, fixable state with concrete next steps, not a stopping point or a reason to fake confidence.

prompt: You're given a small unfamiliar script with no README. What's the most useful first move?

options.text: Find the file that actually gets run first (often named main, index, or app) and read what it does at a glance
Read every file alphabetically from the top
Assume it can't be understood without documentation and stop

hints: Even without a README, the entry point still exists and is still where everything starts.
A README makes orientation faster, but its absence doesn't remove the entry point as a starting place.
explanation: Even with no README, the file that actually runs first still exists and is still the one place everything the program does starts from — reading it first, even without written documentation, gives you a real map to work from. Alphabetical reading and giving up both skip past a genuinely useful starting point.

prompt: A login button does nothing when clicked, in an unfamiliar project. Put these tracing steps in order:

items: Find the click handler attached to the login button
Read what that handler function actually calls
Trace into the function it calls to see where it might be failing silently
Check whether an error is being thrown and swallowed somewhere in that chain

hints: Start from the concrete, observable behavior — the button itself.
A silent failure often means an error is happening somewhere and not being surfaced.
explanation: Starting from the button's own handler and following what it calls, one link at a time, is how you narrow toward wherever the chain silently breaks. A "does nothing" bug is a classic sign of a swallowed error somewhere along that traced path.

prompt: You're searching an unfamiliar project for where a specific error message text is generated. Which search term is most likely to work?

options.text: The exact error message text itself, since it's likely to appear directly in the source code
The word "error", cast as widely as possible
The name of the file you think might be relevant, guessed from its icon

hints: Exact, specific text that's likely to literally exist in source code is the strongest kind of search term.
"error" alone is far too generic in most real codebases.
explanation: An exact error message is often written directly as a string literal in the source — searching for that precise text is one of the most reliable ways to jump straight to the relevant code. "error" alone returns far too much noise, and guessing a filename from an icon isn't a real search strategy at all.

prompt: True or false: a function's name is a reliable, complete description of everything it does.

config.statement: A function's name reliably and completely describes everything it does.
config.rubric: A full answer says false, and explains that a function's real behavior — including any side effects — is only reliably found by reading its actual definition.

hints: Names are written by people and can go out of date or omit details.
Jump-to-definition exists specifically because names aren't a complete, reliable source of truth.
explanation: False. A name is a hint written by a person, and can be incomplete, outdated, or simply not mention side effects the function actually has. The only reliable source of truth for what a function does is its actual current code — which is exactly why jump-to-definition matters more than trusting a name.

prompt: Sort each action by whether it's a safely scoped change or scope creep, given you were asked to fix one specific typo in a label.

items.text: Fixing only the typo in the label text
Also renaming a nearby variable you find confusingly named
Also reformatting the whole file's indentation while you're there
Verifying the label now displays correctly after the fix

hints: A safely scoped change does exactly what was asked, plus verifying it.
Anything beyond the specific ask, however reasonable, is scope creep in this context.
explanation: Fixing the specific typo and verifying it are both within scope — they're exactly what was asked, checked. Renaming a variable and reformatting the file are real improvements in the abstract, but they're additional, unrelated risk bundled into a change that was supposed to be small and specific.

prompt: You fix a bug where a discount showed as 0% instead of 10%. Which verification step would have caught a fix that overcorrects and now shows 10% for every order, even ones with no discount code?

options.text: Running a case that should NOT get the discount, and confirming it correctly still doesn't
Reading the changed line again and confirming it looks correct
Checking that the file compiles without errors

hints: A fix can succeed on the exact case you tested while failing on a case you didn't.
Testing the case that should NOT trigger the behavior is what catches overcorrection.
explanation: Only running a case that should not receive the discount and confirming it still correctly doesn't would catch this specific kind of regression — a fix that works for the case you tested but incorrectly applies to cases it shouldn't. Reading the code again or checking it compiles wouldn't reveal this at all, since the code is syntactically fine either way.

prompt: You're asked to review whether a piece of unfamiliar code is safe to reuse elsewhere in a project. Describe the actual test you'd apply, using this module's distinction between recognizing and understanding.
hints: The test isn't 'does this look familiar' — it's a specific, concrete check.
Think about predicting a real output for a specific input, ideally an edge case.
explanation: A strong answer describes attempting to predict what the code returns for a specific real input — ideally including an edge case (empty input, zero, a boundary value) — without running it, then actually running it to check. Being able to predict correctly is real evidence of understanding; recognizing familiar syntax or general shape is not the same test and doesn't reliably indicate the code is safe to reuse elsewhere.

prompt: You honestly can't predict what an unfamiliar function returns for a negative input. What's the most productive next step?

options.text: Run the function with that specific input as a deliberate, isolated experiment and observe the real result
Assume it probably works fine and move on
Avoid ever using or discussing this function again

hints: Not understanding something yet is fixable with a concrete next step, not a stopping point.
A deliberate, isolated test is exactly how you close this specific gap.
explanation: Running the specific input as a deliberate experiment — separate from making any real change — is exactly how you turn "I don't know" into real, observed knowledge. Assuming it's probably fine skips the actual check; avoiding the function entirely treats a normal, fixable gap as a permanent one.
